#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run a benchmark only when the requested GPUs are exclusively ours, and prove it stayed
# that way.
#
# These boxes are shared and jobs arrive without warning. A run that starts on idle GPUs
# can be sharing them thirty seconds later, and the result looks like a real measurement --
# just a wrong one. Worse, partial contention (2 of 4 ranks slowed) skews a collective
# benchmark in a way that is invisible in the output.
#
# Usage:
#   ./tools/exclusive.sh 4,5,6,7 -- torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 benchmark/bench_a2a.py --mode stages
#   WAIT_SECS=1800 ./tools/exclusive.sh 4,5,6,7 -- <cmd>     # wait up to 30 min for idle
set -uo pipefail

DEVICES="${1:?usage: $0 <gpu list, e.g. 4,5,6,7> -- <command...>}"
shift
[[ "${1:-}" == "--" ]] && shift

WAIT_SECS="${WAIT_SECS:-0}"          # how long to wait for the GPUs to become free
SAMPLE_SECS="${SAMPLE_SECS:-5}"
# One process per GPU is what our own run contributes; anything beyond that is a neighbour.
EXPECT_PER_GPU="${EXPECT_PER_GPU:-1}"

IFS=',' read -ra GPU_LIST <<< "${DEVICES}"

uuid_of() { nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,uuid --format=csv,noheader | awk -F', ' -v i="$1" '$1==i{print $2}'; }

# Processes currently on the requested GPUs.
foreign_count() {
    local total=0
    for idx in "${GPU_LIST[@]}"; do
        local uuid n
        uuid=$(uuid_of "${idx}")
        n=$(nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=gpu_uuid --format=csv,noheader 2>/dev/null |
            grep -c "${uuid}" || true)
        total=$((total + n))
    done
    echo "${total}"
}

# --- 1. wait for idle ---
waited=0
while :; do
    busy=$(foreign_count)
    [[ "${busy}" -eq 0 ]] && break
    if [[ "${waited}" -ge "${WAIT_SECS}" ]]; then
        echo "REFUSED: GPUs ${DEVICES} have ${busy} process(es) on them and did not free up" \
             "within ${WAIT_SECS}s. Not measuring on shared GPUs." >&2
        exit 3
    fi
    sleep 10
    waited=$((waited + 10))
done
echo "# exclusive: GPUs ${DEVICES} idle after ${waited}s wait"

# --- 2. sample while the command runs ---
max_seen=0
min_clock=99999
samples=0
sample_file=$(mktemp /tmp/cno_exclusive_samples.XXXXXX)
# Trap the signals an interrupted ssh actually delivers, not just EXIT: a dropped
# connection leaves the sampler and its temp file behind otherwise, and stale samplers
# then show up as "foreign" processes to the next run.
cleanup() {
    [[ -n "${sampler:-}" ]] && kill "${sampler}" 2>/dev/null
    rm -f "${sample_file}"
}
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM HUP

(
    # Stop if the parent went away, so an orphaned sampler cannot outlive the run.
    parent=$$
    while kill -0 "${parent}" 2>/dev/null; do
        n=$(foreign_count)
        clk=$(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,clocks.sm --format=csv,noheader,nounits |
              awk -F', ' -v list="${DEVICES}" 'BEGIN{split(list,a,",");for(i in a)want[a[i]]=1}
                                               want[$1]{print $2}' | sort -n | head -1)
        echo "${n} ${clk:-0}"
        sleep "${SAMPLE_SECS}"
    done
) > "${sample_file}" &
sampler=$!

# Bind the command to the GPUs we just verified. Without this the script polices one set of
# devices and the run lands on another -- torch defaults to 0..N-1 -- so a VERDICT of
# EXCLUSIVE would say nothing about where the numbers came from. DEVICES is always physical
# indices, matching what nvidia-smi reports; the child sees them renumbered from 0.
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="${DEVICES}"

"$@"
status=$?

kill "${sampler}" 2>/dev/null
wait "${sampler}" 2>/dev/null

# --- 3. verdict ---
while read -r n clk; do
    samples=$((samples + 1))
    [[ "${n}" -gt "${max_seen}" ]] && max_seen="${n}"
    if [[ -n "${clk}" && "${clk}" -gt 0 && "${clk}" -lt "${min_clock}" ]]; then
        min_clock="${clk}"
    fi
done < "${sample_file}"

expected=$((${#GPU_LIST[@]} * EXPECT_PER_GPU))
if [[ "${max_seen}" -gt "${expected}" ]]; then
    echo "# VERDICT: CONTENDED -- saw up to ${max_seen} processes on ${DEVICES}," \
         "expected at most ${expected} (ours). Discard these numbers." >&2
    exit 4
fi
echo "# VERDICT: EXCLUSIVE (${samples} samples, max ${max_seen}/${expected} procs," \
     "min SM clock $([[ ${min_clock} -eq 99999 ]] && echo n/a || echo "${min_clock} MHz"))"
exit "${status}"

1	# Benchmarks
2	
3	Measured 2026-08-08, H100 on 2026-08-09. All five GPU models are in.
4	Read the H100 caveat in "Machines": its two samples are the same node, so its spread is run-to-run
5	variance and not the node-to-node agreement the other four report.
6	
7	Every number here is 0.2.0's, and it still describes the transfer path, which 0.2.1 did not touch.
8	What 0.2.1 added sits above that path and is **not measured**: the staging pool, which lets
9	same-shaped async calls overlap rather than serialise on the caller's stream, and `lend=True`,
10	which drops the copy-out without a caller-owned buffer. Both are correctness-tested and neither
11	has a number, because the method below needs a whole idle node and none was available.
12	
13	## Method
14	
15	Every number is taken under `tools/exclusive.sh`, which refuses to start until the requested GPUs
16	are free, samples throughout, and prints `EXCLUSIVE` or `CONTENDED`. Every run below reported
17	`EXCLUSIVE`. Numbers from different machines are not compared except where the table says so.
18	
19	- **Whole node, 8 GPUs**, allocated exclusively, behind a GPU health gate.
20	- **One binary.** A single wheel built for `80;90;100;120` was installed on every machine
21	  (`sha256 5e4e3747…`), so nothing was recompiled between generations.
22	- **One image**, `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.07-py3` — torch `2.13.0a0+9186a08b2c.nv26.07`,
23	  CUDA 13.3. The one exception is B200's ws=4 rows, noted at "At world_size 4".
24	- **Correctness first.** `pytest test/` passed on each machine before any measurement; a number
25	  from a build that fails its own tests only looks like data.
26	- **Two nodes per model.** v0.1 had to withdraw a published row when a second node of the same
27	  model disagreed by 5×. Where the two nodes agree, one is shown and the spread is noted; where
28	  they do not, both are shown and nothing is averaged.
29	
30	bf16, `mode=0`, medians over 25 iterations after 8 warm-up calls, milliseconds. Shapes are the
31	attention inputs of two real models, QKV packed into one collective so the last dim is
32	`3 * head_dim`. `s` includes a 227-token text tail, so it does not divide by the group size.
33	
34	| label | s | heads | 3·head_dim | MB/rank at ws=8 |
35	|---|---|---|---|---|
36	| wan-720p | 75827 | 40 | 384 | 291 |
37	| wan-480p | 32987 | 40 | 384 | 127 |
38	| h3-t2va-5s | 38051 | 56 | 384 | 205 |
39	
40	```bash
41	benchmark/collect.sh <label>          # everything, with the environment recorded next to it
42	./tools/exclusive.sh 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 -- torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 \
43	    benchmark/bench_a2a.py --mode {stages|zerocopy|sweep|link|zerosm|overlap|padding}
44	```
45	
46	Raw logs, one per (model, node), are archived outside this repo. Each carries its own
47	fingerprint header: driver, torch, CUDA, `nvidia-smi topo -m`, SM clocks before and after, and the
48	commit.

51	
52	| machine | fabric | status |

54	| 8×H200 | NVLink | measured, two nodes agree within 3.9% |
55	| 8×B200 | NVLink | measured, two nodes agree within 7.9% |

87	`all_to_all_single` by 1.16–1.36×.

89	The node-2 spread is not in the transport. Where it reaches 7–8% (B200's two smaller shapes) the
90	`transfer` stage agrees to within 2% and the difference is in the barriers — that is rank arrival
91	skew, which moves between the opening and closing handshake and does not change what was moved.
92	
93	## How much of the fabric this uses
94	
95	Flat 64 MiB peer copies, measured through torch symmetric memory rather than through this operator,
96	so the ceiling is established independently of what is judged against it. The last column is
97	`transfer` at wan-720p over the bytes that actually cross a link (7/8 of 291 MB), against the
98	single-flow number.
99	
100	| GPU | 1 flow | 8 flows, per flow | 8 flows, aggregate | a2a achieves | of the ceiling |
101	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
102	| H200 | 378.7 GB/s | 376.0 | 3008 GB/s | 375 GB/s | **99%** |
103	| B200 | 691.7 GB/s | 689.4 | 5515 GB/s | 621 GB/s | **90%** |
104	| B300 | 692.1 GB/s | 686.9 | 5495 GB/s | 620 GB/s | **90%** |

106	
107	Per-flow bandwidth does not drop when all eight flows run at once, on any of them: the fabric is
108	not the contended resource. At 90–99% of what a flat copy achieves there is essentially nothing
109	left to schedule, which is the useful way to read the `transfer` column above.
110	
111	## The zero-copy path
112	
113	`out=` from `empty_output()` removes the `copy_out` stage, and the saving is the size of that
114	stage: 0.039–0.201 ms saved against a 0.048–0.201 ms `copy_out`. Row by row it lands a little
115	either side, because the two are separate measurements of the whole call, not a subtraction.
116	
117	The last column is `copy_out` as a share of the four timed stages, which is what the benchmark
118	prints; it is not `copy_out / copying`.
119	
120	| GPU | shape | copying | zero-copy | saved | speedup | copy_out, share of the timed stages |
121	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
122	| H200 | wan-720p | 0.911 | 0.790 | 0.121 | **1.15×** | 16.6% |
123	| H200 | wan-480p | 0.418 | 0.351 | 0.067 | **1.19×** | 16.1% |
124	| H200 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.627 | 0.521 | 0.106 | **1.20×** | 16.3% |

126	| B200 | wan-480p | 0.267 | 0.224 | 0.043 | **1.19×** | 17.9% |
127	| B200 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.387 | 0.319 | 0.068 | **1.21×** | 18.3% |
128	| B300 | wan-720p | 0.567 | 0.475 | 0.093 | **1.20×** | 17.6% |

130	| B300 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.388 | 0.320 | 0.068 | **1.21×** | 18.2% |
131	| H100 | wan-720p | 0.934 | 0.733 | 0.201 | **1.27×** | 22.0% |
132	| H100 | wan-480p | 0.440 | 0.344 | 0.095 | **1.28×** | 21.2% |

134	
135	The range is 1.14–1.28× and it tracks the `copy_out` share: the smallest share (B300's wan-480p,
136	15.6%) gives the smallest speedup, and the two largest (H100's wan-480p and wan-720p, 21.2% and
137	22.0%) give the two largest, 1.28× and 1.27×. That is the check that what is being saved is the
138	copy-out and nothing else.
139	H100 gains the most because its copy-out is the largest share of its call: the same
140	device-to-device copy against the slowest fabric here.
141	
142	There is a second reason to prefer it, which the times above do not show: `copy_out` is a
143	same-device copy, and a same-device copy competes with compute for SMs where a peer copy does not
144	(see [design.md](design.md); `--mode zerosm` is the A/B, and it is not in this document — see
145	"What is not measured"). The zero-copy path is the one that is actually zero-SM end to end.
146	
147	## Hiding the collective under compute
148	
149	`hidden% = (serial − concurrent) / a2a_alone`, against a concurrent 3-GEMM chain shaped like
150	to_q/k/v. This is the claim the zero-SM design exists to support.
151	
152	**This metric has real spread.** The two nodes of the same model differ by up to 35 points, and the
153	benchmark prints the min–max of its own eight alternating samples. Read it as a range.
154	
155	| GPU | gemm alone | a2a alone | serial | concurrent | hidden (node 1) | hidden (node 2) |
156	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
157	| H200 | 1.793 | 0.876 | 2.971 | 2.320 | **74%** | 71% |
158	| B200 | 0.978 | 0.535 | 1.633 | 1.312 | **60%** | 95% |
159	| B300 | 0.865 | 0.533 | 1.469 | 1.219 | **47%** | 50% |
160	| H100 | 1.830 | 0.925 | 3.050 | 2.451 | **65%** | 61% |
161	
162	H200 hides more than the Blackwell parts because there is more GEMM to hide under: its
163	`a2a_alone / gemm_alone` is 0.49 against B200's 0.55 and B300's 0.62. The metric is bounded by how
164	much compute is available, not only by how well the collective gets out of the way.
165	
166	## Removing the sequence padding
167	
168	Rounding a sequence up to a multiple of the group size keeps every rank the same length, which is
169	what lets the baseline stay on its flat path; the padded tokens then ride through attention and
170	the collective on every layer of every step. Per-rank `seq_splits` accepts shards differing by one
171	token instead. The pad is at most `world_size − 1` tokens, so the ratio is the number to read.
172	
173	| GPU | shape | base padded | base unpadded | base cost | ours padded | ours unpadded | ours cost |
174	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
175	| H200 | wan-720p | 1.565 | 1.666 | 1.06× | 0.869 | 0.871 | **1.00×** |
176	| H200 | wan-480p | 0.708 | 0.757 | 1.07× | 0.418 | 0.420 | **1.01×** |
177	| H200 | h3-t2va-5s | 1.118 | 1.189 | 1.06× | 0.649 | 0.652 | **1.00×** |
178	| B200 | wan-720p | 1.187 | 1.251 | 1.05× | 0.533 | 0.537 | **1.01×** |
179	| B200 | wan-480p | 0.541 | 0.571 | 1.06× | 0.265 | 0.272 | **1.03×** |
180	| B200 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.851 | 0.896 | 1.05× | 0.390 | 0.394 | **1.01×** |
181	| B300 | wan-720p | 1.178 | 1.238 | 1.05× | 0.534 | 0.538 | **1.01×** |
182	| B300 | wan-480p | 0.538 | 0.569 | 1.06× | 0.267 | 0.273 | **1.02×** |
183	| B300 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.843 | 0.891 | 1.06× | 0.394 | 0.395 | **1.00×** |
184	| H100 | wan-720p | 1.610 | 1.771 | 1.10× | 0.930 | 0.925 | **1.00×** |
185	| H100 | wan-480p | 0.723 | 0.801 | 1.11× | 0.445 | 0.447 | **1.00×** |
186	| H100 | h3-t2va-5s | 1.142 | 1.262 | 1.11× | 0.661 | 0.661 | **1.00×** |
187	
188	Dropping the pad is free here (1.00–1.03×, every shape on every machine) and costs the baseline
189	5–11%, because it cannot stay on flat `all_to_all_single` once shards differ at all: the same one
190	call, but with split sizes, a per-peer reshape and a `cat` after it. That extra relayout is 10–11%
191	on H100, where it is the most expensive relative to the rest.
192	
193	## At world_size 4
194	
195	The tables above are ws=8 throughout. `collect.sh` also runs ws=4, which had not been published.
196	Four of the eight GPUs on one node, certified exclusive by `tools/exclusive.sh` in both cases.
197	B200 on torch 2.11 + CUDA 13; H100 from the same sweep as its ws=8 rows. One node each, so there is
198	no second-node column.
199

201	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

203	| B200 | wan-480p | 0.303 | 0.414 | 0.324 | **1.041** | 0.009 | 0.290 | 0.009 | 0.086 | **0.394** | **2.64×** | 0.429 | 60.3% |
204	| B200 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.482 | 0.644 | 0.516 | **1.642** | 0.011 | 0.429 | 0.011 | 0.133 | **0.584** | **2.81×** | 0.655 | 60.8% |
205	| H100 | wan-720p | 0.747 | 1.328 | 0.793 | **2.868** | 0.012 | 1.136 | 0.009 | 0.389 | **1.545** | **1.86×** | 1.349 | 53.7% |
206	| H100 | wan-480p | 0.331 | 0.642 | 0.350 | **1.323** | 0.010 | 0.510 | 0.008 | 0.172 | **0.701** | **1.89×** | 0.688 | 51.5% |
207	| H100 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.529 | 1.034 | 0.560 | **2.123** | 0.013 | 0.934 | 0.010 | 0.275 | **1.233** | **1.72×** | 0.948 | 51.3% |
208	
209	Both ratios are higher at ws=4 than at ws=8 -- B200's by a lot (2.6-2.8x against 1.9-2.2x), H100's
210	barely (1.7-1.9x against 1.6-1.7x) -- and the reason is the baseline, not this operator. A permute
211	costs the whole tensor whatever the group size, while the collective itself moves only `(ws-1)/ws`
212	of it -- 3/4 here against 7/8 at ws=8. So the relayout the baseline pays and this path does not is
213	a larger share of a smaller total. Read the `relayout%` column, not the multiplier, when comparing
214	across group sizes.
215	
216	## Where this stops being the right tool
217	
218	The barriers cost what they cost regardless of payload, so their share says at which message size
219	to use something else. Most of that cost is rank arrival skew, which any synchronisation pays
220	somewhere — read it as a floor, not as something to optimise away. µs, ws=8, 40 heads, d=384.
221	
222	| GPU | s_local | MB/rank | barr_in | transfer | barr_out | copy_out | total | barriers | GB/s crossed |
223	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
224	| H100 | 16 | 0.5 | 9.3 | 29.8 | 14.4 | 5.1 | 58.6 | **40.4%** | 14.4 |
225	| H100 | 64 | 2.0 | 9.4 | 30.2 | 15.2 | 5.9 | 60.6 | **40.5%** | 57.0 |

236	| H200 | 9478 | 291.2 | 13.3 | 689.2 | 31.7 | 142.9 | 877.2 | **5.1%** | 369.7 |
237	| H200 | 16384 | 503.3 | 11.4 | 1154.7 | 19.2 | 240.1 | 1425.4 | **2.1%** | 381.4 |

252	
253	The share depends on the machine as much as on the size, so read the column, not a rule of thumb.
254	At half a megabyte per rank the handshakes are 33–54% of the call; at 31.5 MB they are 19–34%
255	(B300's 19.4% to B200's 33.9%); at the wan-720p working point (291 MB) they are 5.1–8.4%, and at
256	503 MB, 2.1–6.4% (H200's 2.1% to B300's 6.4%). B200 carries the highest share at every size but
257	the two ends: its `barr_in` sits near 30 µs from `s_local` 64 up, against about 10 µs elsewhere.
258	That is arrival skew on those nodes and not a property of the part — H200's single 28.3 µs at
259	`s_local` 16, which is what takes the top share there, is the same thing on another machine.
260	
261	This operator is built for the long-sequence video DiT case, hundreds of MB per rank, which is the
262	end of that range where the handshakes stop mattering.
263	
264	## Why not PCIe
265	
266	RTX PRO 6000 is measured for a different reason: PCIe, GPUs split 4/4 across two CPU sockets, which
267	is the topology the constructor refuses. Three things came out of it.
268	
269	**The refusal works.** With the default `require_nvlink=True`, `UlyssesGroup()` raised
270	`cuda:0 and cuda:1 are not joined by NVLink`, and `doctor` printed an all-`N` matrix — while
271	`pytest test/` passed 51/51 on the same machine, since the tests construct their groups with the
272	check off. This is the first machine with no NVLink at all that the guard has been run on.
273	
274	That evidence is in the log of the run that was *stopped* by the refusal. The two tables below
275	come from separate runs with `--allow-non-nvlink`, whose logs therefore contain no refusal at all.
276	
277	**The cost of ignoring it, with `--allow-non-nvlink`** — and here the two nodes disagree by 5×, so
278	nothing is averaged:
279	
280	| node | PCIe layout, socket 0 | BASE | transfer | OURS | vs BASE | raw |
281	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
282	| A | 2+2 | 14.933 | 22.848 | 24.090 | 0.62× | 14.026 |
283	| B | 3+1 | 17.525 | 122.250 | 122.750 | 0.14× | 16.540 |
284	
285	**The fabric is not what differs.** Flat 64 MiB peer copies give 54.6 and 55.9 GB/s single-flow,
286	and 52.1 GB/s per flow with all eight running, on *both* nodes. What differs is what the collective
287	extracts from it: 11.2 GB/s on one node and 2.1 GB/s on the other — 20% and 4% of the same ceiling,
288	against 90–99% on every NVLink machine.
289	
290	So the PCIe deficit is not bandwidth. It is that the pitched (strided) copy pattern degrades badly
291	there, and by an amount that depends on the PCIe switch layout: the fast node has its socket-0 GPUs
292	in two pairs, the slow one has three on one switch and one alone.
293	
294	This also revises a v0.1 conclusion. v0.1 measured 119.2 ms on one RTX PRO 6000 node, could not
295	reproduce it on a second, and withdrew the row as a bad node. It reproduces here at 122.25 ms, with
296	a second node at 22.85 ms against v0.1's surviving 22.4 ms. **Both modes are real.** v0.1 also
297	recorded that "a pitched copy runs at 1.00–1.10× a flat one, never slower, on either path" — that
298	was measured on different PCIe machines and does not hold here, where the gap is 25×.
299	
300	## Carried over from v0.1
301	
302	Measured on the NVSHMEM backend, kept as context. A same-machine A/B on 2×H200 put the `transfer`
303	stage within 0.8% across the backend swap, and the v0.2 numbers above land within 1% of the v0.1
304	ones on the machines both saw (B200 wan-720p: v0.1 BASE 1.193 / OURS 0.554, v0.2 1.194 / 0.550).
305	
306	- 8×A100-SXM4-80GB: 1.72–1.87× the `torch.distributed` path, raw/CE 1.12–1.37×.
307	- The collective hid ~105% under a concurrent GEMM chain on A100 (read >100% as fully hidden: the
308	  serial arrangement pays a launch cost the concurrent one avoids).
309	
310	## Alternatives tried and not adopted
311	
312	| alternative | result |
313	|---|---|
314	| One stream per peer, and everything on one stream | Both slower than remote-serialised with the own share on the caller's stream: 2.273 / 1.345 / **1.175** ms at wan-720p, 4×H200. |
315	| Sequential peer order instead of XOR-shift | XOR-shift pairs ranks without coordination; measured at ~14% in a sibling implementation. |
316	| `cudaMemcpy3DBatchAsync` | 0.82 ms, and 1.35 ms with `cudaMemcpyFlagPreferOverlapWithCompute`, against the plain `cudaMemcpy3DAsync` used instead. Also rejects the legacy default stream. |
317	| Fusing single-row copies into 3D | 0.67 → 2.24 ms at `b=2`. Fusion is applied only to multi-row copies for this reason. |
318	| Contiguous per-sender segments instead of strided writes | ~9% below contiguous in a sibling implementation, and not available here regardless: the window is the returned tensor, so there is no local pass to interleave afterwards. |
319	| `cuStreamWriteValue64` / `cuStreamWaitValue64` instead of the spin kernel | Concurrent-GEMM overlap fell from +34% to −28%. See [design.md](design.md) for why `CAN_FLUSH_REMOTE_WRITES`, which an earlier note blamed, is not the reason. |
320	| Publishing the closing flag as a copy-engine write on the transfer stream (NCCL's kernel-less shape) | Measured 3× slower than the barrier kernel it would replace (7× 8 B peer copies ≈ 16 µs against 4–6 µs), and it only moves the publish — the wait stays in a kernel. |
321	| Double-buffering the window to drop the opening barrier | Sound, but worth ~0.7% at the design point: it only helps the copying path, costs 2× window memory, and invalidates the premise of the one adversarial test. |
322	| Cross-socket staging through pinned host memory | 2× the link bandwidth on an Intel PCIe machine, 10% on an AMD one — but it needs the receiver to pull, so it is a new transport with a second handshake. Not built; see [design.md](design.md). |
323	
324	## What is not measured
325	
326	- **The zero-SM A/B on these machines.** `--mode zerosm` — a peer copy and a same-device copy of
327	  the same bytes, each under a GEMM chain matched to its own length, reporting that chain's own
328	  slowdown next to the pair's wall clock — was written after this measurement pass, so no table
329	  here carries it. `collect.sh` runs it, so the next pass will have them.
330	- **End-to-end model impact.** These are microbenchmarks — warm L2, no neighbours competing for
331	  bandwidth. Removing the padding saves attention work and memory this cannot see.
332	- **Beyond `world_size = 8`,** or across nodes. ws=4 is above; ws=2 is not measured.
333	- **A second H100 NODE.** H100 was measured after the rest, and both of its samples came from
334	  the same node. Its 15.0% spread on wan-480p is therefore run-to-run, and says nothing about how
335	  two H100 nodes would agree.

# Benchmarks

Measured 2026-08-08, H100 on 2026-08-09. All five GPU models are in.
Read the H100 caveat in "Machines": its two samples are the same node, so its spread is run-to-run
variance and not the node-to-node agreement the other four report.

Every number here is 0.2.0's, and it still describes the transfer path, which 0.2.1 did not touch.
What 0.2.1 added sits above that path and is **not measured**: the staging pool, which lets
same-shaped async calls overlap rather than serialise on the caller's stream, and `lend=True`,
which drops the copy-out without a caller-owned buffer. Both are correctness-tested and neither
has a number, because the method below needs a whole idle node and none was available.

## Method

Every number is taken under `tools/exclusive.sh`, which refuses to start until the requested GPUs
are free, samples throughout, and prints `EXCLUSIVE` or `CONTENDED`. Every run below reported
`EXCLUSIVE`. Numbers from different machines are not compared except where the table says so.

- **Whole node, 8 GPUs**, allocated exclusively, behind a GPU health gate.
- **One binary.** A single wheel built for `80;90;100;120` was installed on every machine
  (`sha256 5e4e3747…`), so nothing was recompiled between generations.
- **One image**, `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.07-py3` — torch `2.13.0a0+9186a08b2c.nv26.07`,
  CUDA 13.3. The one exception is B200's ws=4 rows, noted at "At world_size 4".
- **Correctness first.** `pytest test/` passed on each machine before any measurement; a number
  from a build that fails its own tests only looks like data.
- **Two nodes per model.** v0.1 had to withdraw a published row when a second node of the same
  model disagreed by 5×. Where the two nodes agree, one is shown and the spread is noted; where
  they do not, both are shown and nothing is averaged.

bf16, `mode=0`, medians over 25 iterations after 8 warm-up calls, milliseconds. Shapes are the
attention inputs of two real models, QKV packed into one collective so the last dim is
`3 * head_dim`. `s` includes a 227-token text tail, so it does not divide by the group size.

| label | s | heads | 3·head_dim | MB/rank at ws=8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| wan-720p | 75827 | 40 | 384 | 291 |
| wan-480p | 32987 | 40 | 384 | 127 |
| h3-t2va-5s | 38051 | 56 | 384 | 205 |

```bash
benchmark/collect.sh <label>          # everything, with the environment recorded next to it
./tools/exclusive.sh 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 -- torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 \
    benchmark/bench_a2a.py --mode {stages|zerocopy|sweep|link|zerosm|overlap|padding}
```

Raw logs, one per (model, node), are archived outside this repo. Each carries its own
fingerprint header: driver, torch, CUDA, `nvidia-smi topo -m`, SM clocks before and after, and the
commit.

## Machines

| machine | fabric | status |
|---|---|---|
| 8×H200 | NVLink | measured, two nodes agree within 3.9% |
| 8×B200 | NVLink | measured, two nodes agree within 7.9% |
| 8×B300 SXM6 | NVLink | measured, two nodes agree within 2.6% |
| 8×RTX PRO 6000 | PCIe, 2 sockets | measured, **two nodes disagree by 5×** — see "Why not PCIe" |
| 8×H100 | NVLink | measured, but **both samples are the same node**, up to 15.0% apart |

8×A100 appears in the v0.1 section and is not re-measured: this cluster has none.

## Where the time goes

`BASE` is `torch.distributed`'s path: permute, `all_to_all_single`, permute. `raw` is
`all_to_all_single` alone — same bytes, no relayout, result in the wrong layout, so it is a
transport floor rather than an alternative. `a2a` against `transfer` is the like-for-like pair.

ws=8. The last column is how far the second node's `OURS` was from the first's.

| GPU | shape | perm_in | a2a | perm_out | BASE | barr_in | transfer | barr_out | copy_out | OURS | vs BASE | raw | raw/CE | relayout% | node 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H200 | wan-720p | 0.358 | 0.826 | 0.385 | **1.569** | 0.011 | 0.680 | 0.025 | 0.143 | **0.860** | **1.82×** | 0.859 | 1.26× | 47.3% | 0.8% |
| H200 | wan-480p | 0.162 | 0.378 | 0.171 | **0.711** | 0.010 | 0.319 | 0.035 | 0.068 | **0.431** | **1.65×** | 0.391 | 1.23× | 46.9% | 3.9% |
| H200 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.254 | 0.590 | 0.273 | **1.117** | 0.010 | 0.490 | 0.019 | 0.100 | **0.619** | **1.80×** | 0.609 | 1.24× | 47.2% | 1.1% |
| B200 | wan-720p | 0.347 | 0.478 | 0.369 | **1.194** | 0.030 | 0.410 | 0.013 | 0.097 | **0.550** | **2.17×** | 0.510 | 1.24× | 60.0% | 1.1% |
| B200 | wan-480p | 0.158 | 0.246 | 0.164 | **0.568** | 0.025 | 0.193 | 0.028 | 0.048 | **0.294** | **1.93×** | 0.263 | 1.36× | 56.7% | 7.1% |
| B200 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.247 | 0.365 | 0.262 | **0.874** | 0.025 | 0.289 | 0.046 | 0.072 | **0.431** | **2.03×** | 0.379 | 1.31× | 58.3% | 7.9% |
| B300 | wan-720p | 0.344 | 0.474 | 0.366 | **1.184** | 0.017 | 0.411 | 0.021 | 0.099 | **0.548** | **2.16×** | 0.493 | 1.20× | 59.9% | 1.3% |
| B300 | wan-480p | 0.156 | 0.227 | 0.163 | **0.546** | 0.011 | 0.199 | 0.044 | 0.048 | **0.302** | **1.81×** | 0.242 | 1.21× | 58.4% | 2.6% |
| B300 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.245 | 0.347 | 0.261 | **0.854** | 0.013 | 0.295 | 0.015 | 0.071 | **0.395** | **2.16×** | 0.360 | 1.22× | 59.3% | 2.0% |
| H100 | wan-720p | 0.379 | 0.837 | 0.400 | **1.616** | 0.016 | 0.715 | 0.040 | 0.201 | **0.971** | **1.66×** | 0.831 | 1.16× | 48.2% | 0.8% |
| H100 | wan-480p | 0.171 | 0.376 | 0.178 | **0.726** | 0.014 | 0.325 | 0.023 | 0.093 | **0.454** | **1.60×** | 0.395 | 1.22× | 48.2% | 15.0% |
| H100 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.270 | 0.595 | 0.284 | **1.148** | 0.015 | 0.511 | 0.026 | 0.140 | **0.692** | **1.66×** | 0.599 | 1.17× | 48.2% | 4.0% |

Across three NVLink generations the shape is the same: **1.60–2.17× the `torch.distributed` path**,
of which 46.9–60.0% is relayout that costs nothing here, and the transfer alone beats a bare
`all_to_all_single` by 1.16–1.36×.

The node-2 spread is not in the transport. Where it reaches 7–8% (B200's two smaller shapes) the
`transfer` stage agrees to within 2% and the difference is in the barriers — that is rank arrival
skew, which moves between the opening and closing handshake and does not change what was moved.

## How much of the fabric this uses

Flat 64 MiB peer copies, measured through torch symmetric memory rather than through this operator,
so the ceiling is established independently of what is judged against it. The last column is
`transfer` at wan-720p over the bytes that actually cross a link (7/8 of 291 MB), against the
single-flow number.

| GPU | 1 flow | 8 flows, per flow | 8 flows, aggregate | a2a achieves | of the ceiling |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H200 | 378.7 GB/s | 376.0 | 3008 GB/s | 375 GB/s | **99%** |
| B200 | 691.7 GB/s | 689.4 | 5515 GB/s | 621 GB/s | **90%** |
| B300 | 692.1 GB/s | 686.9 | 5495 GB/s | 620 GB/s | **90%** |
| H100 | 381.4 GB/s | 377.6 | 3021 GB/s | 356 GB/s | **93%** |

Per-flow bandwidth does not drop when all eight flows run at once, on any of them: the fabric is
not the contended resource. At 90–99% of what a flat copy achieves there is essentially nothing
left to schedule, which is the useful way to read the `transfer` column above.

## The zero-copy path

`out=` from `empty_output()` removes the `copy_out` stage, and the saving is the size of that
stage: 0.039–0.201 ms saved against a 0.048–0.201 ms `copy_out`. Row by row it lands a little
either side, because the two are separate measurements of the whole call, not a subtraction.

The last column is `copy_out` as a share of the four timed stages, which is what the benchmark
prints; it is not `copy_out / copying`.

| GPU | shape | copying | zero-copy | saved | speedup | copy_out, share of the timed stages |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H200 | wan-720p | 0.911 | 0.790 | 0.121 | **1.15×** | 16.6% |
| H200 | wan-480p | 0.418 | 0.351 | 0.067 | **1.19×** | 16.1% |
| H200 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.627 | 0.521 | 0.106 | **1.20×** | 16.3% |
| B200 | wan-720p | 0.554 | 0.464 | 0.090 | **1.19×** | 18.4% |
| B200 | wan-480p | 0.267 | 0.224 | 0.043 | **1.19×** | 17.9% |
| B200 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.387 | 0.319 | 0.068 | **1.21×** | 18.3% |
| B300 | wan-720p | 0.567 | 0.475 | 0.093 | **1.20×** | 17.6% |
| B300 | wan-480p | 0.306 | 0.267 | 0.039 | **1.14×** | 15.6% |
| B300 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.388 | 0.320 | 0.068 | **1.21×** | 18.2% |
| H100 | wan-720p | 0.934 | 0.733 | 0.201 | **1.27×** | 22.0% |
| H100 | wan-480p | 0.440 | 0.344 | 0.095 | **1.28×** | 21.2% |
| H100 | h3-t2va-5s | 0.748 | 0.606 | 0.142 | **1.23×** | 18.5% |

The range is 1.14–1.28× and it tracks the `copy_out` share: the smallest share (B300's wan-480p,
15.6%) gives the smallest speedup, and the two largest (H100's wan-480p and wan-720p, 21.2% and
22.0%) give the two largest, 1.28× and 1.27×. That is the check that what is being saved is the
copy-out and nothing else.
H100 gains the most because its copy-out is the largest share of its call: the same
device-to-device copy against the slowest fabric here.

There is a second reason to prefer it, which the times above do not show: `copy_out` is a
same-device copy, and a same-device copy competes with compute for SMs where a peer copy does not
(see [design.md](design.md); `--mode zerosm` is the A/B, and it is not in this document — see
"What is not measured"). The zero-copy path is the one that is actually zero-SM end to end.

## Hiding the collective under compute

`hidden% = (serial − concurrent) / a2a_alone`, against a concurrent 3-GEMM chain shaped like
to_q/k/v. This is the claim the zero-SM design exists to support.

**This metric has real spread.** The two nodes of the same model differ by up to 35 points, and the
benchmark prints the min–max of its own eight alternating samples. Read it as a range.

| GPU | gemm alone | a2a alone | serial | concurrent | hidden (node 1) | hidden (node 2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H200 | 1.793 | 0.876 | 2.971 | 2.320 | **74%** | 71% |
| B200 | 0.978 | 0.535 | 1.633 | 1.312 | **60%** | 95% |
| B300 | 0.865 | 0.533 | 1.469 | 1.219 | **47%** | 50% |
| H100 | 1.830 | 0.925 | 3.050 | 2.451 | **65%** | 61% |

H200 hides more than the Blackwell parts because there is more GEMM to hide under: its
`a2a_alone / gemm_alone` is 0.49 against B200's 0.55 and B300's 0.62. The metric is bounded by how
much compute is available, not only by how well the collective gets out of the way.

## Removing the sequence padding

Rounding a sequence up to a multiple of the group size keeps every rank the same length, which is
what lets the baseline stay on its flat path; the padded tokens then ride through attention and
the collective on every layer of every step. Per-rank `seq_splits` accepts shards differing by one
token instead. The pad is at most `world_size − 1` tokens, so the ratio is the number to read.

| H200 | wan-720p | 1.565 | 1.666 | 1.06× | 0.869 | 0.871 | **1.00×** |
| H200 | wan-480p | 0.708 | 0.757 | 1.07× | 0.418 | 0.420 | **1.01×** |

no second-node column.

At half a megabyte per rank the handshakes are 33–54% of the call; at 31.5 MB they are 19–34%
(B300's 19.4% to B200's 33.9%); at the wan-720p working point (291 MB) they are 5.1–8.4%, and at

the two ends: its `barr_in` sits near 30 µs from `s_local` 64 up, against about 10 µs elsewhere.
That is arrival skew on those nodes and not a property of the part — H200's single 28.3 µs at
`s_local` 16, which is what takes the top share there, is the same thing on another machine.

This operator is built for the long-sequence video DiT case, hundreds of MB per rank, which is the
end of that range where the handshakes stop mattering.

## Why not PCIe

RTX PRO 6000 is measured for a different reason: PCIe, GPUs split 4/4 across two CPU sockets, which
is the topology the constructor refuses. Three things came out of it.

**The refusal works.** With the default `require_nvlink=True`, `UlyssesGroup()` raised
`cuda:0 and cuda:1 are not joined by NVLink`, and `doctor` printed an all-`N` matrix — while
`pytest test/` passed 51/51 on the same machine, since the tests construct their groups with the
check off. This is the first machine with no NVLink at all that the guard has been run on.

That evidence is in the log of the run that was *stopped* by the refusal. The two tables below
come from separate runs with `--allow-non-nvlink`, whose logs therefore contain no refusal at all.

**The cost of ignoring it, with `--allow-non-nvlink`** — and here the two nodes disagree by 5×, so
nothing is averaged:

| node | PCIe layout, socket 0 | BASE | transfer | OURS | vs BASE | raw |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2+2 | 14.933 | 22.848 | 24.090 | 0.62× | 14.026 |
| B | 3+1 | 17.525 | 122.250 | 122.750 | 0.14× | 16.540 |

**The fabric is not what differs.** Flat 64 MiB peer copies give 54.6 and 55.9 GB/s single-flow,
and 52.1 GB/s per flow with all eight running, on *both* nodes. What differs is what the collective
extracts from it: 11.2 GB/s on one node and 2.1 GB/s on the other — 20% and 4% of the same ceiling,
against 90–99% on every NVLink machine.

So the PCIe deficit is not bandwidth. It is that the pitched (strided) copy pattern degrades badly
there, and by an amount that depends on the PCIe switch layout: the fast node has its socket-0 GPUs
in two pairs, the slow one has three on one switch and one alone.

This also revises a v0.1 conclusion. v0.1 measured 119.2 ms on one RTX PRO 6000 node, could not
reproduce it on a second, and withdrew the row as a bad node. It reproduces here at 122.25 ms, with
a second node at 22.85 ms against v0.1's surviving 22.4 ms. **Both modes are real.** v0.1 also
recorded that "a pitched copy runs at 1.00–1.10× a flat one, never slower, on either path" — that
was measured on different PCIe machines and does not hold here, where the gap is 25×.

## Carried over from v0.1

Measured on the NVSHMEM backend, kept as context. A same-machine A/B on 2×H200 put the `transfer`
stage within 0.8% across the backend swap, and the v0.2 numbers above land within 1% of the v0.1
ones on the machines both saw (B200 wan-720p: v0.1 BASE 1.193 / OURS 0.554, v0.2 1.194 / 0.550).

- 8×A100-SXM4-80GB: 1.72–1.87× the `torch.distributed` path, raw/CE 1.12–1.37×.
- The collective hid ~105% under a concurrent GEMM chain on A100 (read >100% as fully hidden: the
  serial arrangement pays a launch cost the concurrent one avoids).

## Alternatives tried and not adopted

| alternative | result |
|---|---|
| One stream per peer, and everything on one stream | Both slower than remote-serialised with the own share on the caller's stream: 2.273 / 1.345 / **1.175** ms at wan-720p, 4×H200. |
| Sequential peer order instead of XOR-shift | XOR-shift pairs ranks without coordination; measured at ~14% in a sibling implementation. |
| `cudaMemcpy3DBatchAsync` | 0.82 ms, and 1.35 ms with `cudaMemcpyFlagPreferOverlapWithCompute`, against the plain `cudaMemcpy3DAsync` used instead. Also rejects the legacy default stream. |
| Fusing single-row copies into 3D | 0.67 → 2.24 ms at `b=2`. Fusion is applied only to multi-row copies for this reason. |
| Contiguous per-sender segments instead of strided writes | ~9% below contiguous in a sibling implementation, and not available here regardless: the window is the returned tensor, so there is no local pass to interleave afterwards. |
| `cuStreamWriteValue64` / `cuStreamWaitValue64` instead of the spin kernel | Concurrent-GEMM overlap fell from +34% to −28%. See [design.md](design.md) for why `CAN_FLUSH_REMOTE_WRITES`, which an earlier note blamed, is not the reason. |
| Publishing the closing flag as a copy-engine write on the transfer stream (NCCL's kernel-less shape) | Measured 3× slower than the barrier kernel it would replace (7× 8 B peer copies ≈ 16 µs against 4–6 µs), and it only moves the publish — the wait stays in a kernel. |
| Double-buffering the window to drop the opening barrier | Sound, but worth ~0.7% at the design point: it only helps the copying path, costs 2× window memory, and invalidates the premise of the one adversarial test. |
| Cross-socket staging through pinned host memory | 2× the link bandwidth on an Intel PCIe machine, 10% on an AMD one — but it needs the receiver to pull, so it is a new transport with a second handshake. Not built; see [design.md](design.md). |

## What is not measured

- **The zero-SM A/B on these machines.** `--mode zerosm` — a peer copy and a same-device copy of
  the same bytes, each under a GEMM chain matched to its own length, reporting that chain's own
  slowdown next to the pair's wall clock — was written after this measurement pass, so no table
  here carries it. `collect.sh` runs it, so the next pass will have them.
- **End-to-end model impact.** These are microbenchmarks — warm L2, no neighbours competing for
  bandwidth. Removing the padding saves attention work and memory this cannot see.
- **Beyond `world_size = 8`,** or across nodes. ws=4 is above; ws=2 is not measured.
- **A second H100 NODE.** H100 was measured after the rest, and both of its samples came from
  the same node. Its 15.0% spread on wan-480p is therefore run-to-run, and says nothing about how
  two H100 nodes would agree.

309	def _baseline_unpadded(x, pg, ws, rank, seq_splits):
310	    """What usp.py's fast path has to become once the shards differ: the same permutes, but with
311	    split sizes, a per-peer reshape and a cat. Comparing against dist.all_to_all over a list would
312	    be comparing two different baselines, not measuring what the pad costs."""
313	    b, _, h_global, d = x.shape
314	    h_local = h_global // ws
315	    y = x.permute(2, 0, 1, 3).contiguous().flatten()
316	    in_sz = [h_local * b * seq_splits[rank] * d] * ws
317	    out_sz = [h_local * b * sp * d for sp in seq_splits]
318	    recv = torch.empty(sum(out_sz), dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device)
319	    dist.all_to_all_single(recv, y, out_sz, in_sz, group=pg)
320	    chunks, off = [], 0
321	    for sp, size in zip(seq_splits, out_sz, strict=True):
322	        chunks.append(recv[off : off + size].reshape(h_local, b, sp, d))
323	        off += size
324	    return torch.cat(chunks, dim=2).permute(1, 2, 0, 3).contiguous()

446	def run_zerosm(group, pg, rank, ws, args) -> None:
447	    """Whether a copy takes SMs, as an A/B with a control: peer destination against same-device.
448	
449	    Goes through torch symmetric memory rather than through the operator, for the reason run_link
450	    does and one more: the operator's path also contains two barrier kernels and a copy-out, which
451	    are SM work by construction, so a measurement of the whole call cannot attribute anything to
452	    the transfer. Here the two arms differ in one thing -- where the destination lives. At equal
453	    bytes they do not last equally long, so each gets its own chain matched to its own copy; a
454	    chain longer than the copy under it pulls the slowdown towards 1.00x whatever the copy does.
455	    Read each arm's copy column against its gemm column before reading its slowdown.
456	
457	    The GEMM chain's own slowdown is a more direct statement than the pair's wall clock -- it is
458	    the compute's own cost, not bounded by how much compute happens to be available, which is what
459	    --mode overlap's hidden% is. It is not sufficient on its own: a copy the chain starved never
460	    ran under it and leaves the slowdown at 1.00x too, which is why the pair ratio and the
461	    full-competition reference are printed next to it and why the header says to read both. They
462	    are also what docs/design.md quotes.
463	    """
464	    import torch.distributed._symmetric_memory as symm_mem
465	
466	    dev = torch.device("cuda", torch.cuda.current_device())
467	    cur = torch.cuda.current_stream()
468	    cps = torch.cuda.Stream()
469	    lhs = torch.randn((GEMM_N, GEMM_N), dtype=torch.float16, device=dev)
470	    rhs = torch.randn((GEMM_N, GEMM_N), dtype=torch.float16, device=dev)
471	
472	    def gemm_chain(reps):
473	        def go():
474	            for _ in range(reps):
475	                _ = lhs @ rhs
476	
477	        return go
478	
479	    def enqueue(src, dst, reps):
480	        """The copy under test, on its own stream. Nothing joins it back: pair() needs it left in
481	        flight, and alone() adds the join."""
482	
483	        def go():
484	            with torch.cuda.stream(cps):
485	                for _ in range(reps):
486	                    dst.copy_(src)
487	
488	        return go
489	
490	    def alone(copy_go):
491	        def go():
492	            cps.wait_stream(cur)
493	            copy_go()
494	            cur.wait_stream(cps)
495	
496	        return go
497	
498	    def pair(copy_go, gemm_go):
499	        """One concurrent region: the chain on the caller's stream, the copy on its own, with a
500	        mark after the chain so its own time inside the region is read separately. Returns the
501	        region's wall clock and that time.
502	
503	        The chain is queued first because whichever is queued second starts as late as the first
504	        one took the host to submit, and the arms are matched in length, so that much of the chain
505	        then runs uncovered at its alone speed and pulls the slowdown towards 1.00x. A chain is a
506	        few launches where the copy is hundreds, so queueing the chain first makes that lag the
507	        smaller of the two."""
508	        w = Stopwatch(3)
509	        w.mark()
510	        cps.wait_stream(cur)
511	        gemm_go()
512	        w.mark()
513	        copy_go()
514	        cur.wait_stream(cps)
515	        w.mark()
516	        parts = w.read()
517	        return [sum(parts), parts[0]]
518	
519	    label0, img, heads, d, txt = SHAPES[0]
520	    s_total = img + txt
521	    s_total -= s_total % ws
522	    design = args.batch * (s_total // ws) * heads * d * 2  # bytes one rank hands the collective
523	
524	    t_one_gemm = median_ms(gemm_chain(1), args.iters, args.warmup)
525	    if rank == 0:
526	        print(f"# world_size={ws}, gemm is m=n=k={GEMM_N} fp16. Every column is a median over")
527	        print(f"#        {ROUNDS}x{INNER} = {ROUNDS * INNER} samples. The arms alternate, and in")
528	        print("#        an arm the alone measurements alternate with the concurrent region")
529	        print(
530	            f"# one gemm is {t_one_gemm:.3f} ms; `chain` is how many of them ran under that arm's"
531	        )
532	        print("#        copy, chosen so the chain lasts about as long as the copy does, and `xN`")
533	        print("#        on the payload is how many copies both arms were stretched to. The bytes")
534	        print("#        are shared between the arms; the chain is per arm, because the same bytes")
535	        print("#        do not take the same time to reach a peer and to reach local memory")
536	        print("# peer = dst is rank (r+1)%ws's symmetric-memory window, so the copy crosses a link")
537	        print("# same = dst is this rank's own memory. Same bytes, same call, local destination:")
538	        print("#        the only difference between the two arms is where the destination is")
539	        print("# gemm slowdown = the chain's own time with the copy underneath it, over its time")
540	        print("#        alone. 1.00x is 'that copy cost the chain nothing'")
541	        print("# pair ratio = concurrent wall clock / max(copy alone, gemm alone); full comp is")
542	        print("#        (copy + gemm) over the same max, i.e. what perfect competition would cost")
543	        print("# NEITHER COLUMN IS THE RESULT ON ITS OWN. A copy the chain starved also leaves the")
544	        print("#        slowdown at 1.00x: overlapped is 1.00x with a 1.00x pair ratio, starved is")
545	        print("#        1.00x with a pair ratio at full comp. Only the first is the zero-SM one,")
546	        print("#        and it is the pair of columns, read together, that separates them")
547	        print("# Both are diluted whenever copy < gemm, since the uncovered part of the chain runs")
548	        print("#        at its alone speed -- read the copy and gemm columns first")
549	        if ws == 1:
550	            print("#")
551	            print("# world_size=1: there is no peer, so THE PEER ARM IS NOT MEASURED and this run")

553	            print(
554	                "# Two NVLink-joined GPUs are the minimum for the comparison this mode exists for."
555	            )
556	        head = (
557	            f"\n{'payload':<16} {'MB/iter':>8} {'flows':>5} {'arm':<5} {'copy':>8} {'gemm':>8} "
558	            f"{'chain':>5} {'pair':>8} {'pair ratio':>11} {'full comp':>10} {'gemm slowdown':>14}"
559	        )
560	        print(head)
561	        print("-" * (len(head) - 1))

563	    for label, nbytes in ((f"{label0}/rank", design), ("64 MiB", 64 << 20)):
564	        n = nbytes // 2
565	        src = symm_mem.empty(n, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=dev)
566	        src.fill_(1.0)
567	        handle = symm_mem.rendezvous(src, pg)
568	        arms = [("same", torch.empty(n, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=dev))]
569	        if ws > 1:
570	            arms.insert(0, ("peer", handle.get_buffer((rank + 1) % ws, (n,), torch.bfloat16)))
571	
572	        # creps sets the bytes, and both arms move the same bytes. Calibrated on the *fastest* arm
573	        # so the shortest of them still lasts LONG_MS: the same bytes take several times longer to
574	        # reach a peer than this rank's own memory, so one copy count cannot make both arms last
575	        # the same. Both payloads are stretched, the design one included -- a single copy of it is
576	        # shorter than one GEMM, and a chain cannot go below one, so both arms would overshoot

589	        rows = [(1, rank == 0)] + ([(ws, True)] if ws > 1 else [])
590	        for flows, mine in rows:
591	            copies = {name: enqueue(src, dst, creps if mine else 0) for name, dst in arms}
592	            # One chain per arm, matched to that arm's own copy, which is the experiment
593	            # docs/design.md describes: a chain "of the same duration". A chain longer than the
594	            # copy under it pulls the slowdown towards 1.00x whatever the copy does, and with one
595	            # shared chain that would hit the same-device arm -- the one that is supposed to
596	            # move -- hardest, since it is the shorter of the two at equal bytes. The calibration
597	            # only has to survive rounding to an integer chain length, so it is a short one.
598	            calib = {a: median_ms(alone(c), INNER, 1) for a, c in copies.items()}
599	            plan = torch.tensor(
600	                [max(1, round(calib[a] / t_one_gemm)) for a in copies],
601	                device=dev,
602	                dtype=torch.int64,
603	            )
604	            dist.broadcast(plan, 0)
605	            greps = dict(zip(copies, plan.tolist()))
606	            chains = {a: gemm_chain(greps[a] if mine else 0) for a in copies}
607	            # Every reported number is sampled inside this loop: the arms alternate, and within an
608	            # arm the concurrent region alternates with the two alone measurements it is divided
609	            # by. A baseline taken once, before the loop, would put the whole run's drift straight
610	            # into the slowdown column. The barrier keeps every rank in the same arm at the same
611	            # time, which is what makes the all-pairs row an all-pairs measurement.

613	            for _ in range(ROUNDS):

617	                    g = median_ms(chains[name], INNER, 1)
618	                    samples[name].append(
619	                        [c, g] + median_of(lambda: pair(copies[name], chains[name]), INNER, 1)
620	                    )
